definition.text: A way of doing statistics that uses Bayes' theorem to work out how likely a hypothesis is from earlier evidence, and to update that probability as new information arrives.

facts.text: It starts from a prior distribution, the belief about a parameter before any data are seen, and turns it into posterior probabilities.
Updating is especially useful when data arrive in a sequence: the posterior from one stage becomes the prior for the next.
It is used in science, engineering, philosophy, medicine, sport, psychology and law.
Abraham Wald showed that every unique Bayesian procedure is admissible, which made Bayesian methods central even to frequentist estimation and hypothesis testing.
In Bayesian model comparison, the model with the highest posterior probability given the data is chosen.
Complex models often cannot be solved in closed form, so Bayesian analysis leans on Monte Carlo simulation such as Gibbs sampling and Metropolis–Hastings.
The name honours Thomas Bayes (1701–1761), but Pierre-Simon Laplace introduced what is now called Bayes' theorem.
Early Bayesian inference was called inverse probability because it reasons backwards from effects to causes.

definition.text: The process of working out the real, separate effect of one thing that is part of a larger system.

facts.text: Unlike finding an association, it asks how an outcome responds when one of its causes is changed.
One description: establish that cause and effect vary together, that the cause comes first, and rule out other plausible causes.
It is especially hard where experiments are difficult or impossible, which is common in most sciences.
In economics and politics it is hard because real economies are complex and many large events cannot be recreated in controlled experiments.
Because correlation does not imply causation, the work is as much about plausible causal mechanisms as about patterns in data.
Economists increasingly use natural experiments and quasi-experimental designs, and randomized field experiments help deal with confounding.
Many social scientists adopted Donald Rubin's potential outcomes framework as a standard for inferring causality.
Critics say economists and social scientists often pass off descriptive studies as causal ones.

title: Confounding variable

definition.text: A variable that strongly affects a study's results but is not the thing whose effect the study is trying to measure.

facts.text: A confounder can make a factor look important in one version of a model and unimportant in another.
A third factor that causes both A and B, making A and B move together, is a confounding variable.
Assigning units to treatments at random tends to balance known and unknown confounders between groups on average.
In impact evaluation, confounding often comes from socioeconomic factors linked both to who receives a programme and to the outcome.

notes: No crawled page of its own; defined on Causal inference and used on Correlation does not imply causation, Design of experiments, Endogeneity and Impact evaluation.

definition.text: A study that tests a cause-and-effect claim without a true controlled experiment, used when a real experiment is not available.

facts.text: Experiments may be too costly, impossible for large systems such as economies, or dangerous to the people involved.
Treatments in quasi-experiments are given as if at random, for example in elections won by very slim margins.
Without controlled experiments, econometricians often look for natural experiments or apply quasi-experimental methods.

definition.text: When two explanatory variables in a model are very highly correlated with each other.

facts.text: Small changes in highly correlated data can flip a variable's estimated effect from positive to negative or back.
Spotting it in a sensitivity analysis lets researchers drop highly correlated variables and avoid such dramatic swings in results.

definition.text: The principle that two things moving together, on its own, does not show that one causes the other.

facts.text: Treating a correlation as proof of cause is a logical fallacy, known in Latin as cum hoc ergo propter hoc, 'with this, therefore because of this'.
Showing a cause usually needs four things: a correlation, the cause coming first, a plausible mechanism, and ruling out common or alternative causes.
A hidden third factor can cause both observed variables, making them move together without either causing the other.
Two unrelated variables can correlate by chance, and the more things are examined the more such accidental links turn up.
Dismissing correlation entirely is the opposite mistake, since much scientific evidence rests on variables observed together.
Assumptions are always needed to draw causal conclusions, and modern causal inference focuses on testing how strong those assumptions are.
In environmental medicine many links could long only be described as correlations because studies that show causation are hard or impossible to run.
The 'credibility revolution' in economics used better methods to tell correlation from causation.

title: Reverse causation
article: Correlation does not imply causation#B causes A (reverse causation or reverse causality)

definition.text: The mistake of reading cause and effect the wrong way round, treating the effect as the cause.

facts.text: Seeing that windmills turn faster when there is more wind does not mean windmills make wind; wind makes them turn.
Low cholesterol goes with higher death rates partly because diseases such as cancer lower cholesterol and also raise mortality.
Two things can each partly cause the other, such as poverty and lack of education.
Where controlled experiments cannot settle the direction of causation, as often in the social sciences, the confusion can fuel long scientific arguments.

definition.text: Planning procedures that test how changing one part of a system leads to changes in other parts.

facts.text: It decides which parts of a system to change and which to hold fixed, based on hypotheses about what drives variation.
The changed inputs are independent variables, and the outcomes they are expected to change are dependent variables.
Main concerns are validity, reliability and replicability, along with enough statistical power.
Ronald Fisher set out a method for designing experiments in The Arrangement of Field Experiments (1926) and The Design of Experiments (1935), much of it for agriculture.
Charles S. Peirce stressed randomization-based inference in publications of 1877–1878 and 1883.
Only when participants are randomly chosen and randomly assigned can differences in outcomes be confidently put down to the different conditions.
Laws and ethics rule out some well-designed experiments on people, through review boards, informed consent and confidentiality.
Choice experiments used to value environmental goods depend on an experimental design that controls which hypothetical scenarios respondents see.

definition.text: Putting people or units into the groups of an experiment by chance, so each has the same chance of ending up in any group.

facts.text: Random assignment is what separates a true experiment from an observational study or quasi-experiment.
It does not remove confounding variables, but it tends to balance known and unknown confounders between groups on average.
Comparing treatments against a control or standard treatment as a baseline is usually more valuable than isolated measurements.
Without random assignment, outcome differences between groups are likely due to some third variable.

definition.text: Trying many analyses, often unconsciously, until one gives the result the researcher wanted.

facts.text: It usually means adjusting the analysis until a result falls below the p<.05 level of statistical significance.
False positives often come from pressure to publish or the author's own confirmation bias.
Preregistration, sending the analysis plan to a journal before collecting data, can prevent it.
Double-blind designs, where researchers do not know who is in which group, stop them influencing participants' responses.

definition.text: A quasi-experimental technique that estimates a treatment's effect by comparing how much a treated group changed over time with how much an untreated control group changed.

facts.text: It needs data on both groups from at least one period before the treatment and at least one after.
Because the groups may start at different levels, it subtracts the 'normal' gap that would exist without treatment; the rest is the treatment effect.
It is a special version of ordinary least squares, and the same estimate comes from a regression with group, period and interaction dummies.
Card and Krueger's 1994 study compared fast-food jobs in New Jersey and Pennsylvania after New Jersey raised its minimum wage, and found no fall in employment.
In environmental economics it is used to assess regulations on pollution, energy use and climate policy.
Richard Hornbeck used it in 2012 to show that heavily eroded Dust Bowl counties lost 20 to 30 percent of land values and farm revenues, with little recovery 10 years later.
It can still suffer from biases such as mean regression, reverse causality and omitted variable bias, depending on how the treated group is chosen.

definition.text: The assumption in difference in differences that, without the treatment, the treated and control groups would have changed by the same amount over time.

facts.text: It fails when something other than the treatment changes in one group but not the other at the same time.
Researchers often combine difference in differences with matching on similar pre-treatment histories to make the assumption more likely to hold.
The two groups' membership is also assumed to stay the same over time.

definition.text: In econometrics, the problem that arises when an explanatory variable is correlated with the model's error term.

facts.text: Put simply, the supposed cause is also being influenced by the outcome, as when education raises income but income also affects education.
It makes an analysis misjudge cause and effect, so the results are unreliable.
It comes from simultaneity, an omitted confounding variable, or explanatory variables measured with error.
When it is present, ordinary least squares gives biased regression coefficients.
Common fixes are instrumental variables, which are correlated with the problem variable but not with the error term, and Heckman selection correction.
It is often overlooked in non-experimental research, which weakens causal claims and policy advice.

definition.text: Endogeneity that arises when two variables are determined together, each affecting the other.

facts.text: The idea comes from simultaneous equations models, which separate variables set inside the model (endogenous) from those fixed in advance (exogenous).
Ignoring simultaneity gives biased and inconsistent estimates.

definition.text: Endogeneity caused when an explanatory variable cannot be measured perfectly, so the observed value carries noise.

facts.text: The noise ends up in both the regressor and the error term, so ordinary least squares underestimates the effect.
Error in measuring the outcome variable does not cause endogeneity, though it makes the error term more variable.

definition.text: An assumption that a model's error term averages zero given the present and past values of the explanatory variables.

facts.text: It allows errors to be correlated with future values of the regressors, so outcomes can feed back into later causes.
Strict exogeneity, which also rules out links with future values, is often implausible in macroeconomic and financial data, so weak exogeneity is the standard there.
Jean-François Richard formalized it in 1980.

definition.text: A regression model for grouped data in which each group's average is treated as a fixed quantity rather than a random draw.

facts.text: In panel data, the fixed effects are each subject's own average, one unchanging intercept per subject.
They control for omitted variable bias from unobserved differences between subjects that stay constant over time, such as innate ability or a country's history and institutions.
These constant differences are removed by subtracting each group's average over time or by taking first differences.
Random effects models assume the subject-specific effects are uncorrelated with the explanatory variables; fixed effects models allow them to be correlated.
Random effects estimates are more efficient when their assumption holds but inconsistent when it does not; the Durbin–Wu–Hausman test is used to choose.

definition.text: A way of removing unchanging individual effects from panel data by regressing each period's change in the outcome on the change in the explanatory variables.

facts.text: With two time periods it gives exactly the same result as the fixed effects estimator.
Fixed effects is more efficient when errors are well behaved; first differences is more efficient when errors follow a random walk.

definition.text: Assessing how far a project, programme or policy actually caused the outcomes seen, intended or not.

facts.text: Unlike monitoring whether targets were met, it asks how outcomes would have changed had the intervention not happened.
It answers evidence-based policy questions: what works, what doesn't, where, why and for how much.
Randomized field experiments are the strongest designs when feasible; otherwise evaluators use quasi-experimental methods such as matching, differencing and instrumental variables.
Whatever design is chosen, every one can yield biased estimates of a programme's effects.
The best-known early large-scale experimental evaluation was of Mexico's Progresa conditional cash transfer programme.
Theory-based evaluation maps the causal chain from inputs to outcomes rather than only reporting average differences between groups.

definition.text: Comparing what actually happened with what would have happened without an intervention.

facts.text: The counterfactual is the outcome beneficiaries would have had without the intervention; impact is the gap between it and what was observed.
The key difficulty is that the counterfactual can never be observed directly, so it must be approximated using a comparison group.
Comparison groups can be set up in advance (prospective) or found afterwards (retrospective).
In difference in differences, the control group stands in for the counterfactual.

title: Randomistas debate

definition.text: The argument over whether randomized experiments should be the main way to evaluate development programmes.

facts.text: William Easterly called it 'The Civil War in Development economics'.
Supporters, called 'randomistas', say randomization is the only way to deal with unobservable selection bias.
Critics say random assignment rarely suits development interventions and gives results for one context with little wider relevance.

contested_note: Proponents of experimental methods and of broader methodologies openly disagree about how development programmes should be evaluated.

definition.text: Changes that would happen anyway during a programme, such as long-term trends, short-term events or people ageing, and that can bias estimates of its effect.

facts.text: A fertility programme may look effective simply because the community's birth rate was already falling.
A health programme for adults may look ineffective because health generally declines with age.
Keeping programme and control groups in comparable circumstances prevents this bias.

title: Systematic review
article: Impact evaluation#Systematic reviews of impact evidence

definition.text: A structured assessment of all existing evidence on a topic, presented in an accessible way to link research and policy.

facts.text: It follows a protocol that sets out in advance which studies to include, how to search and how to combine results.
It can also combine qualitative information, such as barriers to a programme working.
Systematic reviews, sometimes with meta-analyses, are generally ranked as the highest level of evidence in scientific and medical research.
They aim to be rigorous and transparent so that bias in the findings can be assessed and, where possible, reduced.

definition.text: A quasi-experimental method for estimating cause and effect when controlled experiments are not possible, using a third variable that shifts the cause but not the outcome directly.

facts.text: It is needed when an explanatory variable is correlated with the error term, which makes ordinary least squares biased.
A valid instrument changes the explanatory variable, has no effect of its own on the outcome, and is uncorrelated with the error term.
To study smoking and health, the tobacco tax rate can serve as an instrument, assuming it affects health only through smoking.
Philip G. Wright first used an instrument in a 1928 book, trying to estimate supply and demand for butter; Olav Reiersøl named the method in 1945.
Whether an instrument is truly unrelated to the error cannot be read from data and must come from understanding how the data were generated.
When effects differ between people, the standard estimate recovers a local average treatment effect rather than the population average.

title: Two-stage least squares
article: Instrumental variables#Interpretation as two-stage least squares

definition.text: A way to calculate instrumental-variable estimates by running two regressions in turn.

facts.text: First, each problem explanatory variable is regressed on all the exogenous variables, including the instruments, to get predicted values.
Second, the main regression is run with those predicted values in place of the problem variables.

definition.text: Instruments that predict the problem explanatory variable poorly, which undermines an instrumental-variables estimate.

facts.text: If smoking hardly responds to tobacco taxes, tax variation reveals nothing about smoking's effect on health.
A common rule of thumb is that the first-stage F-statistic should be larger than 10.

definition.text: A statistical model for yes-or-no outcomes that treats the log-odds of the event as a weighted sum of explanatory variables.

facts.text: It uses the S-shaped logistic function to turn a combination of inputs into a probability between 0 and 1.
Its coefficients are usually estimated by maximum likelihood, using an iterative method because no closed-form answer exists.
It is used in machine learning, most medical fields and the social sciences.
Logit models of discrete choice can be estimated by logistic regression, and are used to analyse choice-based survey tasks.
Multinomial logistic regression extends it to outcomes with more than two categories.
A common alternative is the probit model.
A widely used rule of thumb asks for about 10 events per explanatory variable for stable estimates.
With its upper limit set to 1, the logistic function's output lies between 0 and 1 and can be read as a probability.

title: Log-odds
article: Logistic regression#Definition of the inverse of the logistic function

definition.text: The logit: the natural logarithm of the odds of an event, the inverse of the logistic function.

facts.text: In logistic regression the log-odds equal the linear regression expression, so the logit links probabilities to a linear model.
The odds of the outcome equal the exponential of the linear regression expression.

definition.text: A way of estimating the parameters of an assumed probability distribution by choosing the values that make the observed data most probable.

facts.text: Its logic is intuitive and flexible, and it has become a dominant way of doing statistical inference.
Except in special cases the equations cannot be solved directly and must be solved step by step from an initial guess.
With enough data it is consistent, homing in on the true parameter value with arbitrary precision.
It matches the most probable Bayesian estimate when the prior over the parameters is uniform.
Predictions from it ignore the uncertainty in the estimated parameters.
Ronald Fisher created the modern method between 1912 and 1922, building on Gauss, Laplace and others.
Discrete choice, probit and logit models are typically estimated this way.

definition.text: A method for combining the numerical results of many independent studies of the same research question.

facts.text: Its core step is computing a combined effect size from the studies' effect sizes and variances.
Pooling studies increases statistical power and can settle disagreements between individual studies.
Gene V. Glass coined the term in 1976 as 'the analysis of analyses', though Karl Pearson pooled typhoid inoculation studies in 1904.
A fixed effect model weights studies by the inverse of their variance, so large studies dominate; a random effects model allows true effects to differ between studies.
It cannot fix poor design or bias in the original studies, which argues for including only sound studies.
A 2020 meta-analysis of 180 studies found no evidence of the decoupling of growth from environmental harm needed for ecological sustainability.
A 2021 meta-analysis of 3186 estimates rejected the Cobb–Douglas production function.
Its core step is computing one combined effect size across all the studies.

title: Publication bias
article: Meta-analysis#Publication bias: the file drawer problem

definition.text: The distortion that arises because studies with negative or insignificant results are less likely to be published, so published evidence exaggerates effects.

facts.text: Pharmaceutical companies have hidden negative studies, and unpublished dissertations or conference abstracts are easily overlooked.
It is hard to fix because no one can know how many studies went unreported.

A 2026 meta-analysis of 2,193 estimates from 88 economics experiments found that, after correcting for publication bias, financial incentives have a mean effect on performance close to zero in most field settings.

definition.text: A family of computer methods that get numerical answers by repeated random sampling.

facts.text: The idea is to use randomness to solve problems that are not random in themselves.
Its main uses are optimization, numerical integration and drawing samples from probability distributions, especially for problems with very uncertain inputs.
The simplest version estimates an average by running many simulations and averaging their results.
It is named after the Monte Carlo Casino; Stanisław Ulam, its main developer, was inspired by his uncle's gambling.
It can be very costly to compute, but the runs are independent, so they can be spread across many processors.
In cost–benefit analysis it supports formal risk analysis of uncertain costs and benefits.
The IPCC relies on it to analyse probability distributions of radiative forcing.
Unlike 'what if' scenarios built on best-guess values, it samples each uncertain variable from a probability distribution to produce hundreds or thousands of possible outcomes.

definition.text: A study in which nature or other forces outside the researchers' control decide who is exposed to a condition and who is not.

facts.text: The exposure may resemble random assignment, but natural experiments are observational studies, not controlled ones.
They are most reliable when a clear exposure hits a well-defined group while a comparable group stays unexposed.
They are used when controlled experiments would be extremely difficult or unethical, as often in epidemiology and economics.
John Snow's study of the 1854 Broad Street cholera outbreak, comparing water drawn above and below London's sewage outfalls, is one of the best-known early examples.
Angrist used the Vietnam War draft lottery as an instrumental variable and found veterans earned about 15 percent less than non-veterans.
When air pollution fell in the twentieth century, dark forms of the peppered moth quickly became scarce again, a large-scale natural experiment in natural selection.
Inability to control variables can stop investigators from drawing firm conclusions.

definition.text: The error that arises when a statistical model leaves out a relevant variable, so its effect is wrongly credited to the variables that were included.

facts.text: It needs two conditions: the left-out variable affects the outcome, and it is correlated with an included explanatory variable.
The estimate then mixes the direct effect of the included variable with an indirect effect running through the omitted one.
It breaks the ordinary least squares assumption that errors are uncorrelated with the regressors, making estimates biased and inconsistent.
If the omitted variable is positively related to both a regressor and the outcome, that regressor's effect is overstated.
Fixed effects models can remove it when the unobserved differences stay constant over time.

definition.text: The standard way to fit a linear regression: choose the parameters that make the sum of squared gaps between observed and predicted values as small as possible.

facts.text: Each gap between a data point and the fitted line is a residual; the sum of squared residuals measures how well the model fits.
Some sources treat it as the same thing as linear regression.
By the Gauss–Markov theorem it is the best linear unbiased estimator when errors have equal variance and are uncorrelated.
If errors are normally distributed, it gives the same answer as maximum likelihood.
Its key assumption is that the regressors are uncorrelated with the errors.
With a constant and one explanatory variable it is the 'simple regression model' taught in beginner statistics.
Cobb and Douglas used least squares to estimate a labour exponent of 0.75 for their production function.

definition.text: Data that follow the same subjects, such as people, firms or countries, with repeated measurements over time.

facts.text: Time series (one subject over time) and cross-sectional data (many subjects at one time) are one-dimensional special cases of panel data.
In a balanced panel every subject is observed in every period; in an unbalanced panel some are missing.
Unchanging subject traits such as a country's geography or climate cause omitted variable bias in ordinary least squares if they are correlated with explanatory variables.
Fixed effects and first-difference estimators can control for such traits; random effects is more efficient when they are uncorrelated with the regressors.
Using a lagged outcome as a regressor creates dynamic panel data, where instrumental variables or GMM methods such as the Arellano–Bond estimator are needed.
A panel of 130 countries from 1975 to 2010 found obesity rising with income in poor settings and falling in rich ones.

definition.text: Poisson regression is a form of regression analysis built to model counts, such as how many times an event happens.

facts.text: It assumes the outcome follows a Poisson distribution and that the logarithm of its expected value is a linear combination of unknown parameters.
When an explanatory variable rises by 1, the predicted count is multiplied by the exponentiated coefficient, called the incidence ratio.
It also handles rates, such as tree species per unit area, by adding the logarithm of exposure as an offset term.
Its parameters are estimated by maximum likelihood, which has no closed-form answer and must be found numerically.

definition.text: Overdispersion is when count data vary more than their mean, breaking the Poisson model's assumption that the mean equals the variance.

facts.text: A common cause is leaving out relevant explanatory variables, or observations that depend on each other.
Negative binomial regression loosens the equal mean and variance assumption and is a popular alternative.
Excess zeros arise when one process decides whether any events happen and another decides how many, as with non-smokers in a survey of cigarettes smoked.

definition.text: Program evaluation is a systematic way of collecting and using information to judge whether projects, policies and programs work and whether they are good value for money.

facts.text: Funders, voters and others often need or want to know whether the programs they support are producing the promised effect.
It overlaps with cost-benefit analysis, but social outcomes can be harder to assess than market outcomes and need different skills.
An evaluation can examine needs, the program's theory, its implementation, its impact and its efficiency, at different stages of the program's life.
The hardest part is often showing that the program itself, rather than outside events, caused the observed changes.
Many projects include no budget for evaluation, and an evaluation started late may have no baseline data from before the program began.
Additionality may be checked after the fact, as program evaluation often does, or beforehand as a screen for issuing environmental credits.

definition.text: A program theory, or logic model, is the assumption built into a program's design about how its actions will lead to the outcomes it wants.

facts.text: Program staff often leave the logic model unstated, so an evaluator must draw it out of them and judge whether it is plausible.

definition.text: Reliability is how far a measure gives the same result each time it measures the same thing; validity is how far it measures what it is meant to measure.

facts.text: A poorly chosen measure can undermine an impact assessment completely by producing misleading estimates.
The more reliable a measure is, the greater its statistical power and the more credible its findings.
A measure must also be sensitive enough to detect the changes a program might cause.

title: Propensity score matching

definition.text: Propensity score matching is a way to estimate a treatment's effect from observational data by comparing treated and untreated units that were equally likely to be treated, given their observed characteristics.

facts.text: Paul Rosenbaum and Donald Rubin introduced it in 1983, defining the propensity score as the probability of being assigned to treatment given observed covariates.
It tries to mimic randomization by building treated and untreated samples that look alike on all observed covariates.
The score is usually estimated with logistic regression, then each participant is matched to one or more similar non-participants and covariate balance is checked.
Collapsing many covariates into one score let it balance groups without needing huge samples, avoiding the dimensionality problem.
It only accounts for observed covariates, so hidden bias from unobserved factors can remain after matching.
It needs large samples with substantial overlap between treatment and control groups.

contested_note: Some research finds that propensity score matching increases imbalance, inefficiency, model dependence and bias, and Judea Pearl argues matching can even raise hidden bias.

title: Back-door criterion
article: Propensity score matching#Graphical test for detecting the presence of confounding variables

definition.text: The back-door criterion is Judea Pearl's graphical test for spotting confounding variables in a causal diagram.

facts.text: To estimate a treatment's effect, the background variables must block every back-door path in the graph.
A path can be blocked by adding the confounder as a control in a regression or by matching on it.

definition.text: A randomized controlled trial (RCT) is an experiment that tests an intervention by assigning participants to comparison groups at random, which limits bias.

facts.text: At least one group gets the intervention, while others get an alternative, a placebo or standard care.
Proper randomization removes bias in who gets treated, specifically selection bias and confounding.
RCTs are seen as the most reliable evidence in healthcare because they reduce spurious causality and bias, and their results can be pooled in systematic reviews.
If a treatment's effect is small, too few participants may make it impossible to reject the null hypothesis.
They can be costly: 28 Phase III trials funded by one US institute before 2000 cost US$335 million in total, a mean of US$12 million each.
Withholding an obviously beneficial treatment from a control group can make an RCT unethical.
Jan Baptist van Helmont first proposed an RCT, to compare two fever treatments, in a book published in 1648.

title: Randomized controlled trials in economics

definition.text: In economics, randomized controlled trials have become a standard way to identify causal effects, especially in development economics.

facts.text: In 1994 Paul Glewwe, Michael Kremer and Sylvie Moulin began one of the earliest economic RCTs, a long-run school intervention in Kenya.
RCTs helped bolster the credibility revolution in empirical microeconomics.
Since 2013 the American Economic Association registry has tracked over 7,400 field experiments across 100 countries.

contested_note: Economists and other social scientists remain divided over how far RCTs should be used in their fields.

definition.text: Blinding means keeping participants, caregivers or outcome assessors from knowing which intervention each person received.

facts.text: A placebo in the control group lets participants stay unaware of which treatment they got.
Blinding is sometimes impossible, as when a treatment such as physical therapy needs the patient's active participation.

definition.text: Regression analysis is a statistical method for estimating how an outcome variable relates to one or more explanatory variables.

facts.text: Its most common form is linear regression, which finds the line or plane that best fits the data by some mathematical rule.
Ordinary least squares picks the line that minimizes the sum of squared differences between the data and the line.
A regression model has unknown parameters, observed explanatory variables, an observed outcome variable and unobserved error terms.
By itself a regression is just a calculation; treating it as a model of real relationships needs assumptions such as a representative sample and error-free explanatory variables.
Including several variables in a regression isolates the effect of one of them, which mirrors the economist's idea of holding other things constant.
Legendre published the method of least squares in 1805 and Gauss in 1809, and Francis Galton coined the term regression in the 19th century.

definition.text: In linear regression the outcome is modelled as a linear combination of the parameters, though not necessarily of the explanatory variables themselves.

facts.text: Simple linear regression has one explanatory variable; multiple linear regression has several.
Linear regression can model curved relationships by adding transformed predictors such as squared terms, because it only needs to be linear in the parameters.
A residual is the gap between the value the model predicts and the true value of the outcome.
Least squares estimates come from solving a set of simultaneous linear equations called the normal equations.

definition.text: Regression assumptions are the classical conditions researchers rely on to read a regression as a meaningful model of real-world relationships.

facts.text: They include a representative sample, explanatory variables measured without error, errors averaging zero given the covariates, and constant error variance, called homoscedasticity.
If errors are not normally distributed, estimated parameters in small samples will not be normal either, which complicates inference.

definition.text: Regression diagnostics are checks of how well a fitted regression model matches the data and whether its estimated parameters are statistically significant.

facts.text: Common checks of fit include R-squared, the pattern of residuals and hypothesis tests.
Significance is checked by an F-test of overall fit followed by t-tests of individual parameters.
How these tests should be read depends heavily on the model's assumptions.

definition.text: A limited dependent variable is an outcome that is categorical or confined to a certain range, a common situation in econometrics.

facts.text: Running least-squares regression on a yes-or-no outcome gives the linear probability model.
Nonlinear models for yes-or-no outcomes include the probit and logit models, and the multinomial logit handles categories with more than two values.

definition.text: Extrapolation is using a regression model to predict outside the range of the data it was fitted on; predicting inside that range is interpolation.

facts.text: The further a prediction goes beyond the data, the more room the model has to fail.
Extrapolation leans especially hard on the assumed form of the relationship, which can only be checked within the observed range.

definition.text: A regression discontinuity design is a quasi-experimental method that estimates an intervention's effect by comparing cases just above and just below the cutoff that decides who gets it.

facts.text: If every student scoring above 80% gets a scholarship, students at 79% and 81% are likely very similar, so comparing them reveals the scholarship's local effect.
Simply comparing award winners and non-winners would overstate the effect, because strong students both win awards and keep doing well.
Donald Thistlethwaite and Donald Campbell first used it in 1960 to evaluate scholarship programs.
It requires that people cannot perfectly manipulate which side of the cutoff they land on, so assignment near the threshold is as good as random.
Done well, it can give treatment effect estimates similar to randomized studies without the ethical issues of random assignment.
Its estimates can be wrong if a curved relationship is mistaken for a jump, or if another treatment shares the same cutoff.
Other uses include age eligibility rules such as pensions or drinking ages, and elections won by a narrow majority.

title: Testing regression discontinuity validity
article: Regression discontinuity design#Testing the validity of the assumptions

definition.text: Regression discontinuity validity tests look for evidence that cases just above and just below the cutoff are not truly comparable.

facts.text: McCrary's density test checks for a bunching of observations at the threshold, such as more students just passing than just failing, a sign of gaming.
Variables fixed before treatment, such as earlier grades, should show no jump at the cutoff.
Unexpected jumps at other points of the assignment variable also make the design suspect.

definition.text: A fuzzy regression discontinuity design handles cutoffs that are not strictly applied, needing only that the chance of treatment changes at the threshold.

facts.text: Real cutoffs are often bent, for instance by discretion for students just short of passing, which biases a sharp design.
Its logic is related to the instrumental variable strategy and intention to treat.

definition.text: A regression kink design identifies treatment effects from a sharp change in the slope, rather than the level, of a treatment rule such as student aid that depends on family income.

facts.text: Nielsen, Sørensen and Taber named the technique in 2010.

definition.text: The Rubin causal model is a way of analysing cause and effect in which a treatment's effect is the difference between the outcomes a unit would have with and without it, its potential outcomes.

facts.text: A person would have one income at age 40 if they went to college and another if they did not; the causal effect compares the two.
Jerzy Neyman first proposed potential outcomes in his 1923 master's thesis, and Donald Rubin extended the idea to observational as well as experimental studies.
Randomized experiments can estimate causal effects for a population, because random assignment makes groups equivalent on average.
The average treatment effect is the mean of all the individual causal effects.
How units are assigned to treatment matters: a 'perfect doctor' who gives each patient whatever suits them best distorts the comparison of averages.
A causal effect is only well defined if both outcomes could happen; height cannot be manipulated, so its causal effect on weight makes no sense in this framework.

title: Fundamental problem of causal inference
article: Rubin causal model#The fundamental problem of causal inference

definition.text: The fundamental problem of causal inference is that we can never observe both potential outcomes for the same unit, so individual causal effects cannot be seen directly.

facts.text: A patient cannot both take a pill and not take it over the same period.
This does not make causal inference impossible; certain techniques and assumptions get around it.
Assumptions are needed to estimate the missing counterfactual outcomes.

title: Stable unit treatment value assumption
article: Rubin causal model#Stable unit treatment value assumption (SUTVA)

definition.text: The stable unit treatment value assumption (SUTVA) requires that one unit's outcome is unaffected by which treatment other units receive.

facts.text: If Mary's drug makes her cook with more salt, Joe's blood pressure depends on her treatment too, violating SUTVA.
Field experiments call it the non-interference assumption.
Violations make causal inference harder, though dependence can be handled by considering more treatments.

definition.text: Selection bias arises when the people, groups or data chosen for analysis are picked in a way that makes the link between exposure and outcome differ from the link among everyone eligible.

facts.text: It typically occurs when researchers condition on a factor influenced by both the exposure and the outcome, creating a false association.
It includes loss to follow-up, volunteer bias, healthy-worker bias and nonresponse bias.
Volunteers may differ from the target population; studies find they tend to come from higher social standing.
In general it cannot be fixed by analysing existing data alone, though Heckman correction works in special cases.
Researchers' choices of where to study may bias modern estimates of biodiversity.

definition.text: Sampling bias is systematic error from a non-random sample in which some members of a population are less likely to be included than others.

facts.text: It is usually treated as a kind of selection bias, though some classify it separately.
One view holds that sampling bias threatens how far results generalize, while selection bias mainly threatens comparisons within the sample.
Examples include self-selection and pre-screening of trial participants.

definition.text: Attrition bias is selection bias caused by losing participants, such as dropouts and non-responders, during a study.

facts.text: In a diet trial, dropping everyone who quits biases results, because most quitters are those for whom the diet was not working.
It is closely related to survivorship bias, where only subjects that survived a process are analysed.

definition.text: Sensitivity analysis studies how the uncertainty in a model's output can be traced back to, and shared among, the uncertain inputs that feed it.

facts.text: Models in fields like climate science or economics can be so complex that how their inputs drive their outputs is poorly understood.
Inputs can be uncertain because of measurement errors, missing information, poor understanding of mechanisms or the choice of underlying hypothesis.
It is almost always done by running the model many times with sampled inputs, which can be computationally expensive.
In cost-benefit analysis, a sensitivity analysis shows how the results respond when parameters change.
The European Commission, the US Office of Management and Budget, the IPCC and the US EPA include sensitivity analysis in their guidelines.
Leamer's global sensitivity analysis judges conclusions sturdy only if a credibly wide range of assumptions still gives a usefully narrow range of inferences.

title: Uncertainty analysis

definition.text: Uncertainty analysis describes the overall uncertainty in a model's output, while sensitivity analysis asks which input uncertainty matters most.

facts.text: It focuses on quantifying uncertainty and how it propagates through a model, and ideally runs alongside sensitivity analysis.

notes: No page of its own; drawn from the Sensitivity analysis lead and Related concepts section.

definition.text: One-at-a-time sensitivity analysis changes a single input while holding the others at baseline values, to see how the output responds.

facts.text: The input is then returned to its baseline value and the step is repeated for each other input.
Like local derivative-based methods, it examines small changes one variable at a time and does not explore the full range of inputs.

definition.text: Variance-based sensitivity analysis treats inputs and outputs as random variables and splits the output's variance into shares caused by each input and combination of inputs.

facts.text: The shares are calculated as Sobol indices, the proportion of output variance explained by an input or group of inputs.
The first-order index measures one input's contribution alone, averaged over variations in the others.

definition.text: Sensitivity auditing extends sensitivity analysis to the framing, institutional context and motives behind a model whose results feed policy decisions.

facts.text: Framing can carry implicit assumptions, from political ones such as which group needs protecting to technical ones such as which variable is treated as constant.

definition.text: Spatial econometrics is the field where spatial analysis and econometrics meet, handling models in which places interact or observations are not truly independent.

facts.text: It estimates models with spatial autocorrelation or neighbourhood effects, common in regional science, real estate and housing markets.
It analyses economic effects such as externalities, interactions and spatial concentration.
Belgian economist Jean Paelinck introduced the term in May 1974.

title: Statistical hypothesis test

definition.text: A statistical hypothesis test uses sample data to decide whether a claim about a population, such as a drug lowering blood pressure, holds up.

facts.text: It builds a model of what the data would look like if chance alone produced the results, then asks how likely the actual data are under that model.
If the data are very unlikely under the null hypothesis, it is rejected; if not, the only conclusion is that the evidence against it is insufficient.
Because a sample cannot settle the truth for certain, a test's conclusion can be wrong.
Modern significance testing comes mainly from Karl Pearson, William Sealy Gosset and Ronald Fisher, while Jerzy Neyman and Egon Pearson developed hypothesis testing.
John Arbuthnot first used it in 1710, testing whether male and female births in London were equally likely.
A test is like a court trial: the null hypothesis, like the defendant, is presumed true until evidence shows otherwise.

notes: The dossier's Definition line (S:9de165479fc6) is a table caption, not a definition; definition built from the Definition of terms section.

title: Null hypothesis
article: Statistical hypothesis test#Technical description of the null hypothesis

definition.text: The null hypothesis is the default claim that a measured quantity, usually a difference or effect, is zero.

facts.text: A test weighs the null hypothesis against its negation, the alternative hypothesis.
For a heart-attack drug, a possible null hypothesis is that the drug has no effect on the risk of a heart attack.
Paul Meehl argued that when the null is simply 'no effect', a more precise experiment is a less severe test of the theory behind it.

distinct_from: Type I and type II errors

title: P-value

definition.text: A p-value is the probability of getting a test result at least as extreme as the one observed if the null hypothesis were true.

facts.text: If the p-value is at or below the test's significance level, written alpha, the null hypothesis is rejected.
A rejection does not mean the chance that the null hypothesis is true is below alpha.
The threshold is usually set so that results this extreme would occur less than 5% or 1% of the time under the null.
Statistical significance does not imply practical significance.

distinct_from: Type I and type II errors

title: Type I and type II errors

definition.text: A type I error rejects a null hypothesis that is actually true (a false positive); a type II error keeps a null hypothesis when the alternative is true (a false negative).

facts.text: The probability of a type I error equals the test's significance level.
One minus the probability of a type II error is called the test's power.
A typical randomized trial accepts a 0.05, or 1 in 20, chance of wrongly finding two equally effective treatments different.
Large samples are recommended to reduce type II errors.

title: Criticism of significance testing

definition.text: Critics of null hypothesis significance testing argue it is misunderstood, overused and misused, and should not be the only tool of statistical analysis.

facts.text: Modern practice is a hybrid of Fisher's and Neyman and Pearson's approaches, which critics say causes confusion.
Rigidly requiring significance for publication produces publication bias.
Many critics prefer estimation statistics, reporting an estimated value with an interval rather than an accept-or-reject verdict.
Critics would ban it completely, while supporters prefer a less absolute change.

contested_note: Critics and supporters agree on how significance testing works but disagree over whether to abandon it or reform it.
distinct_from: Type I and type II errors

definition.text: The synthetic control method builds a comparison group for a treated unit from a weighted average of untreated units, recreating the path the treated unit would have followed without the intervention.

facts.text: It is often used when only one or a few units, such as a region, are treated.
Weights are chosen from the data so the synthetic control closely matches the treated unit on key predictors, usually over a long period before the intervention.
Unlike difference in differences, it can account for confounders that change over time.
It combines elements of matching and difference in differences, and was first proposed by Alberto Abadie and coauthors.
Applications include natural catastrophes and economic growth, vaccine mandates, and drug development where randomized trials are not feasible.

definition.text: A truncated regression model handles samples from which observations above or below certain values of the outcome have been systematically left out.

facts.text: Whole observations are missing, unlike censored models where the explanatory variables are still known.
In the 1970s James Heckman linked truncated samples to other non-randomly selected samples and developed the Heckman correction.
These models are usually estimated by maximum likelihood.
